title: Oxidation states and naming; Born–Haber cycles and lattice enthalpy
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: RX02#t3 term and clue written for the game; RX02#t2 term and clue written for the game; RX02#t1 term and clue written for the game; EN06#t3 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EN06#N.4, RX02#N.4a, EN06#N.13, RX02#N.8, RX02#N.10.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Metal hydride
items.clue: Compound such as NaH or CaH₂ in which H is −1.

items.label: Peroxide
items.clue: Compound such as H₂O₂ or Na₂O₂ in which O is −1.

items.label: Oxidation number
items.clue: The charge an atom would have if all its bonds were ionic.

items.label: First electron affinity
items.clue: ΔH when 1 mol of gaseous atoms each gain one e⁻: Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g).

questions.stem: Which equation, with the sign of its enthalpy change, represents the enthalpy change of lattice formation of sodium chloride?
questions.explanation: One mole of solid forms from its gaseous ions. The ions attract, so energy is released: negative.

questions.stem: What are the oxidation numbers of hydrogen in sodium hydride, NaH, and of oxygen in sodium peroxide, Na₂O₂?
questions.explanation: In NaH, Na is +1, so H is −1 (the hydride ion). In Na₂O₂, 2(+1) + 2x = 0, so O is −1 (the peroxide ion, O₂²⁻).

questions.stem: For which compound would you expect the largest percentage difference between the Born–Haber lattice enthalpy and the value from a perfect ionic (purely electrostatic) model?
questions.explanation: Mg²⁺ is small and doubly charged, so it polarises strongly. I⁻ is large, so its electron cloud is easily distorted. Most covalent character, biggest gap.
2(+1) + 2x + 7(−2) = 0 gives 2x = +12, so each Cr is +6. The numeral is per atom.

questions.stem: Chlorine is −1 in the chloride ion, Cl⁻, but +1 in the hypochlorite ion, ClO⁻ (in bleach). Which explains the +1?

options.text: The chlorine atom in ClO⁻ has lost a proton to the oxygen atom, leaving chlorine with a +1 charge.
Oxygen always has the oxidation number −1 in an ion with one negative charge.
Oxygen is more electronegative than chlorine, so it is assigned the shared electrons in the Cl–O bond.
The chlorine atom in ClO⁻ carries a real charge of +1, as in a Cl⁺ ion.

questions.explanation: O takes both shared electrons and is −2; the total must be −1, so x + (−2) = −1 and Cl is +1. In Cl⁻, chlorine holds an extra electron: −1.
